extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical geometry; readers of Archimedes; mathematicians studying conoids, spheroids, and classical plane/solid geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and applying Archimedes' treatise material: definitions, lemmas, and propositions about circles, conoids, spheroids, ellipses, parabolas, and related constructions and area/volume ratios. Includes constructive existence results (cones/cylinders through a given ellipse), metric inequalities, and comparison propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of circle area with K (comparison proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the area of the circle is neither greater nor less than K, it is equal to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses inscribed/circumscribed polygons and properties that perpendicular from centre to polygon side equals radius while polygon perimeter > circle circumference; uses bisection and tangent constructions to derive contradictions if area differs. (Surrounding text gives the limiting polygon approximation process.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2 (area to square on diameter ratio—text flagged)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of a circle is to the square on its diameter as 11 to 14.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes this proposition statement is 'not satisfactory' and that Archimedes could not have placed it before the later proposition on which the approximation depends; the book signals that the arithmetic content and approximations require careful treatment (see Introduction, Ch. IV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3 (circumference to diameter bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the circumference of any circle to its diameter is less than 22/7 but greater than 223/71.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes constructs regular polygons (inscribed and circumscribed, up to 96 sides) by successive angle bisections and gives chained inequalities for chord/tangent lengths to bound the circumference; intermediate arithmetic approximations and certain steps are supplied or summarized (many steps are omitted in the Greek text and indicated in square brackets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: right-angled conoid (paraboloid of revolution) and basic segment notions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a section of a right-angled cone (a parabola) is revolved about its diameter (axis) and returned, the resulting figure is a right-angled conoid; axis is the fixed diameter; tangent planes and parallel cutting planes define segments with 'base', 'vertex', and 'axis' of the segment as specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology is given literally from the Greek; subsequent propositions rely on these precise definitions (e.g., comparing segment to cone with same base and axis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for right-angled conoid
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) If a segment cut by a plane at right angles to the axis, it is half again as large as the cone with same base and axis. (2) If two segments cut off by any planes, their areas are in the duplicate ratio of their axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the motivating problems for the section; proofs follow using geometrical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: obtuse-angled conoid (hyperboloid of revolution) and related terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a section of an obtuse-angled cone (a hyperbola) is revolved about its diameter, the nearest lines (asymptotes) generate an enveloping isosceles cone; the conoid, its axis, vertex, enveloping cone, and the 'line adjacent to the axis' are defined; segments and bases are likewise defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions for obtuse-angled conoids relate segment measures to cones via ratios involving the axis and the adjacent line; similarity of such conoids is tied to similarity of their enveloping cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for obtuse-angled conoid
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) A right-angled cut segment bears to the cone (same base and axis) the ratio: (axis + 3×adjacent_line) : (axis + 2×adjacent_line). (2) Same ratio holds when cutting not at right angles: the segment bears to the corresponding conical segment this ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give explicit algebraic ratios connecting conoid segments and cones; the definitions of 'adjacent to the axis' and construction of enveloping cone are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: spheroidal figures (oblong and flat) and segment similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblong spheroid: revolution of section of acute-angled cone about its major diameter; flat spheroid: revolution about minor diameter; axis, vertex, centre, and diameter are defined. Parallel tangent planes and parallel cutting planes define segments whose bases, vertices, and axes are specified. Similarity of spheroids is defined by axis:diameter ratios; similarity of segments when cut from similar bodies with similar bases and axes ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precise definitions underpin the later theorems about area and proportion relations of spheroids and their segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for spheroids (summary problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple problems: (1) Sections through centre at right angles: each segment double cone with same base/axis; (1a,b) cuts not through centre give ratios expressed by sums involving half the spheroid axis and segment axes; (2,3) analogous statements for cuts not perpendicular to axis — many cases and explicit ratio statements involving halves and sums of axes. Also problems on triplicate ratios of axes and relations between diameters and axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerate the target theorems: triplicate ratio of axes for similar spheroids, reciprocal proportionality of squares on diameters to axes, and construction problems (cut off a segment equal to a given cone/cylinder/sphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: segment of a cone (ἀπότμαμα κώνου) and frustum of a cylinder
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cone is cut by a plane meeting all generators and the section is an ellipse, the portion towards the vertex is a segment of a cone; its base is the plane of section, vertex is cone vertex, axis joins vertex to centre of the section. A cylinder cut by two parallel planes with ellipse sections yields a frustum with axes joining centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These geometric object definitions are used in later ratio comparisons (e.g., frustum triple of conical segment of same base/height).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (arithmetic progression inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: If in an ascending arithmetic progression A1, A2, ... , An the common difference equals the least term A1, then n * A_n < 2(A1 + A2 + ... + An) and > 2(A1 + A2 + ... + An) (text gives demonstration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes provides an incidental proof using line placements; this lemma is used in subsequent algebraic-sum inequalities and propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1 (ratio property of series of magnitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given series of magnitudes with proportional corresponding terms (B_i : B_j = B'_i : B'_j etc.), sums of the series hold corresponding compounded ratio equalities: (A1+ B1+ ... +K1) : (A2+ B2+ ... +K2) = (A1 + B'1 + ... ) : (A2 + B'2 + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by equating pairwise ratios and using ex aequali; includes corollary that omission of corresponding terms preserves result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma to Proposition 2 (sum of squares identity for arithmetic progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1, A2, ... , An form an ascending arithmetic progression with common difference equal to A1, then (n+1)A_n^2 + A1(A1 + A2 + ... + An) = 3(A1^2 + A2^2 + ... + An^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes proves by constructing and extending lines and algebraically manipulating sums; corollaries relate to substitution of squares by similar figures (duplicate ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2 (inequalities for areas expressed via applied rectangles)
rubrics_metrics.description: For areas A_i formed by applied rectangles (following method of application of areas), inequalities comparing n * A_n and sums of A_i are given, producing bounds of the form n*A_n : (sum of A_i) < (a + n a) : (5 + ...) etc. (paraphrased from detailed arithmetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses previous lemmas and translates arithmetic progression results into geometric-area inequalities; Archimedes emphasizes traditional application-of-areas language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8(1) (tangents and parallel chords in conics)
rubrics_metrics.description: If TP and TP' are two tangents to any conic meeting at T, and QQ and Q'Q' are chords parallel respectively to TP and TP' meeting at O, then OT : OO' = TP^2 : TP'^2 (proved in elements of conics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes refers to earlier conic treatises (Aristaeus, Euclid) for proof; the identity relates chord distances to tangent lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8(2) (parabola: constant area of triangle and segment for fixed parameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: If QQ' is a chord of a parabola bisected in V by the diameter PV, and PV is of constant length, then the areas of triangle PQQ' and of the parabola segment PQQ' are both constant regardless of chord direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses parameter p of principal ordinates and relations QV^2 = p * PV; Archimedes references Quadrature of the Parabola results for segment area being 4/3 of triangle area (Prop. 17 or 24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4 (area of an ellipse relative to auxiliary circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of any ellipse is to that of its auxiliary circle as the minor axis to the major axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume auxiliary circle area greater or less and compare inscribed polygons in circle and ellipse; uses correspondence of perpendiculars cut on axis and proportional triangles/trapezia to show impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5 (area ratio of ellipse to arbitrary circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AA', BB' are major and minor axes of ellipse and d is diameter of any circle, then (area of ellipse) : (area of circle) = AA' * BB' : d^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Prop. 4 and area scaling of circles: area(ellipse) : area(auxiliary circle) = BB' : AA', and area(auxiliary circle) : area(circle with diam d) = AA' : d^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6 (areas of ellipses proportional to rectangles under axes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas of ellipses are as the rectangles under their axes (i.e., area ∝ major_axis × minor_axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct corollary of Props. 4 and 5; implies that similar ellipses areas are as squares of corresponding axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7 (existence of cone through ellipse with given vertex O)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse with centre C and a line CO perpendicular to its plane, it is possible to find a circular cone with vertex O whose surface passes through the circumference of the ellipse (i.e., the ellipse is a section of that cone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: choose circle with appropriate diameter BD in plane perpendicular to ellipse plane, form cone with BD base and vertex O; algebraic/comparative length equalities show any point P on ellipse lies on cone generator (use right-triangle and product relations QM^2 = HM·MK = PN^2 = ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8 (alternate cone construction through ellipse when OA ≠ OA')
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse and a plane through one axis perpendicular to the ellipse plane and a line CO drawn in that plane (not perpendicular to axis), one can construct a cone with vertex O whose surface passes through the ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: produce OA' to D so OA = OD, draw AD and parallel FG through C, choose an appropriate circle or ellipse on AD as axis, then build cone with vertex O through that circle/ellipse; show any point P on ellipse meets cone generator via proportional equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9 (existence of cylinder through ellipse with given axis OC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse, a plane through one axis perpendicular to ellipse plane, and line OC drawn from centre C in that plane (not perpendicular to axis), one can find a cylinder with axis OC whose surface passes through the ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three cases depending on relation of other axis to DE (constructed line): (1) BB' = DE: build circle on DE as diameter and cylinder; (2) BB' > DE: choose DE' so DE' = BB' and proceed; (3) BB' < DE: pick K on OC produced and construct perpendicular KR equal to CB', then circle on DE as diameter passing through R; in each case show point P on ellipse corresponds to generator of cylinder using product equalities PN^2 = DM·ME = QM^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10 (ratio of cones and frusta; cylinder-frustum relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two cones have ratio compounded of ratios of their bases and heights; same method shows any segments of cones have ratio compounded of bases and heights. Also any frustum of a cylinder is triple of the conical segment with same base and equal height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Euclid XI results and classical proofs (Eudoxus); references to On the Sphere and Cylinder and Euclid for background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11 (paraboloid sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) A paraboloid of revolution cut by a plane through or parallel to the axis yields a parabola equal to the generating parabola; axis of section is intersection between plane of section and plane through paraboloid axis at right angles to cutting plane. If cut at right angles to axis, section is a circle centered on axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the nature of planar sections of paraboloids (parabolic or circular) and locates their axes/centres; used in subsequent solids/volume considerations.
